package_info.package_versions: All versions after attacker takes over the abandoned username/repository
package_info.why_malicious: The package repository can be hijacked by an attacker after the original owner changes their GitHub username, allowing the attacker to publish malicious code under the original package path. This enables highly effective supply chain attacks on all downstream consumers and transitive dependencies, especially in high-privilege admin tools, by introducing malicious code that executes automatically upon import.

execution_context.file_location: any .go source file in the hijacked package (e.g., logrus.go)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At import-time, the code enumerates running processes, encodes and exfiltrates process names to a remote C2 server via HTTP GET, receives and executes remote commands from the server, and if unsuccessful, writes and executes an embedded OS-specific binary payload as a secondary stage, resulting in system compromise.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code initiates process enumeration, exfiltrates sensitive process information to an external domain, executes arbitrary commands received from a remote server, and drops and runs an embedded binary payload. These actions are hallmarks of malware, especially when triggered automatically at import-time without user interaction.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: A legitimate Go package, particularly a utility or logging library, should not perform process enumeration, data exfiltration, remote command execution, or drop and execute binaries during import/init. Such behaviors are not expected and violate the principle of least privilege and user consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Process enumeration may be used in legitimate monitoring or diagnostic tools, but never as part of a logging or utility library and never automatically at import-time. Remote command execution and payload dropping are not legitimate in this context.
key_indicators: init() function triggers malicious actions at import-time
Remote command execution based on C2 server response
Process enumeration for anti-analysis or reconnaissance
Automatic execution of OS-specific binaries from package code

attack_chain.action: Attacker claims abandoned GitHub username and publishes a malicious package under the original repository path.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious package is available for import by downstream projects.

attack_chain.action: Developers or CI systems import the hijacked package (directly or as a transitive dependency).
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code is included in the build and executed at import-time.

attack_chain.action: Malicious init() function executes: collects process info, exfiltrates data, receives and executes remote commands, and drops additional payloads.
attack_chain.leads_to: Compromise of developer or production systems, potential lateral movement or further payload deployment.

behavioral_signatures: Go package init() functions performing network requests at import-time
Process enumeration at import-time in utility or logging libraries
HTTP requests to suspicious or non-standard domains (e.g., badguy.com) during build or import
Remote command execution triggered by C2 server response in Go dependencies
Dropping and executing embedded binaries (e.g., via go-binddata) from Go packages during import
file_indicators: Presence of unexpected init() functions in Go dependencies
References to go-binddata or embedded binary payloads in Go source files
Unexpected changes in go.mod/go.sum pointing to previously trusted but now hijacked repositories
Go source files (e.g., logrus.go) containing process enumeration and network exfiltration code
network_indicators: Outbound HTTP requests to attacker-controlled domains (e.g., badguy.com)
Unusual network activity from build or test environments during go build or go test phases
HTTP GET requests with base64-encoded process information as query parameters
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for Go package dependencies that have changed ownership or repository paths, especially those previously considered trusted. Use static analysis to scan imported Go packages for init() functions that perform network activity, process enumeration, or command execution. Flag any Go package that makes outbound HTTP requests or drops/executes binaries at import-time. Monitor for changes in go.mod/go.sum that point to previously trusted but now hijacked repositories. Implement network monitoring to detect HTTP requests to known attacker-controlled domains (e.g., badguy.com) originating from build or CI environments.
